title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
summary: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.

title: Latent-Predisposition Personas for Heterogeneous and Reliable LLM Survey Simulation
summary: LLM personas are used to simulate survey publics, which should reproduce not only answer distributions but also within-person coherence and stability. Drawing on mass belief systems research, we show that persona-conditioned LLMs produce over-constrained publics. Across three model families and three U.S. surveys, opinions on unrelated issues are 1.6-4.6 times as correlated as among humans, and party identification explains 2.5-7.6 times as much answer variance. Common remedies (temperature, diversity instructions, backstories) weaken these correlations by making answers more random. On Qwen, their ten-day test-retest reliability falls to 33-59% of the human level, and when made consistent they lose correlation fit. We propose Latent-Predisposition Personas (LPP), whose persons differ stably, not randomly. Each persona receives political engagement, value priorities, and party-relative issue deviations that grow as engagement falls. Answers are sharpened and calibrated to toplines and party crosstabs. At selected operating points, LPP is never significantly worse than any baseline and far more reliable. At matched human-level reliability, it has the lowest correlation error in all six model-survey combinations, also at a lower target. Errors still exceed those between human samples, and gains on framing effects and a frontier closed model are partial.

title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
summary: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.

title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
summary: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.

title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
summary: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.

title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
summary: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
summary: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

title: probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
summary: As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.

title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
summary: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.

title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
summary: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
summary: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

title: Reinforcement Learning from LLM-Generated (Suboptimal) Demonstrations
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved substantial progress across many domains, but training an agent \textit{tabula rasa} remains highly sample-inefficient. A common remedy is to initialize the agent using a neural network pretrained on demonstrations. However, collecting demonstrations is expensive, and the demonstrations themselves can be suboptimal. In this work, we use a large language model (LLM) to generate an advice policy that produces demonstration data with effectively no human cost. We use this data to warmstart a DQN agent, and use the advice policy itself to guide exploration during training. Because LLM-generated advice is often suboptimal, we further introduce a value warmstart method that initializes the agent to recognize promising states from the advice policy's behavior, without directly copying its actions. To characterize the robustness of this method, we systematically perturb individual sub-skills of an LLM-generated advice policy for a long-horizon, sparse-reward task. Degraded advice still meaningfully accelerates learning relative to unaided baselines. These results suggest that LLM-generated advice, though suboptimal, can be a cheap alternative to costly human demonstrations.

title: Reasoning Beyond Imitation: Observation Conditioned Distillation for Video LLMs
summary: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
summary: Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence. However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.

title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
summary: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.

title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.

title: Where Do Fact-Checking Errors Arise? Separating Retrieval, Search Control and Judgement in Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: An evidence-grounded fact-checker can fail because it does not find the evidence or because it does not use it; end-to-end accuracy does not tell the two apart. We present a protocol that follows the reference evidence from the store to the verdict and separates retrieval, search control, judgement and verdict validation. We assess 293 claims from FEVER, FEVER 2.0 and AVeriTeC with one open-weights 9B model under two evidence conditions: small stores of annotated evidence, where discovery is easy, and the full source collections. In the control condition a single hybrid retrieval pass delivers complete reference evidence for 226 of 228 evidence-bearing claims, and adaptive controllers and a tool agent spend two to nine times as many model calls without a consistent gain. Of 34 decisive claims labelled as lacking evidence, 33 have the complete evidence in the packet: in 15 the judge abstains, and in 18 validation rules overturn a decisive verdict. On AVeriTeC these rules lower single-pass accuracy by six points, to 65.0% (balanced accuracy 57.6%). Ten judges from eight model families also show abstentions and validation conversions on fixed packets. Against the full stores hybrid single-pass accuracy falls by 17 to 29 points. Wikipedia evidence recovery declines; AVeriTeC recovery changes from annotated answers to cited pages and is measured separately. No controller recovers the accuracy loss. The agent also shows no resolved gain on 714 further Wikipedia claims. Evidence recovery, judgement and validation should be measured separately before an error is attributed to search.

title: Do More Roles or Larger Models Improve LLM Fact-Checking? A Controlled Study on Fixed Evidence
summary: A fact-checking system can spend more computation on a claim by using a larger model, by asking the same model several times, or by a multi-role Tribunal: two roles propose quoted findings, code checks the quotations, an auditor that does not see the proposed relation judges each one, and code derives the verdict or abstains. We compare these options on identical fixed evidence, without retrieval: 300 AVeriTeC claims, each with its annotated question--answer items mixed with items written for other claims, read by judges of four open-weights models from three families, a vote of five, and six assignments of models to the Tribunal's roles. The 9B judge was right on 186 claims and the 27B judge of the same family on 156; the larger judges declined to decide far more often and were no more accurate when they decided. The vote reached 196 and the 9B judge with its verdict replaced by Tribunal certificates 195, at a similar cost; the Tribunal alone reached 153 to 164, because it abstained on almost half of the claims. A hearing's outcome followed the auditor's model and was nearly indifferent to the proposers'. A larger auditor, or one of another family, made certificates neither more often correct (77% to 81%) nor more independent of the judge. As a replacement, certificates improved every judge by 3 to 10 points and overturned four to five in a hundred of its correct verdicts. With the annotated evidence withheld, judges and Tribunal still decided on 7% to 14% of the claims.

title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
summary: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.

title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
summary: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.

title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
summary: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.

title: Reducing Authorship Attribution Risk in Student Texts Through Style-Conditioned Rewriting
summary: Building NLP applications for education is constrained by data scarcity due to student privacy concerns and data regulations. To address this, we propose a style-aware approach to rewriting student forum posts that retains analytical value while reducing identifiability. Our method isolates content, structure, and style as separate conditioning channels and aggregates over student-disjoint exemplar partitions within style clusters, extending Differentially Private In-context Learning (DP-ICL) with cluster-restricted retrieval. Across three educational NLP datasets, our approach achieves high style fidelity, preserves downstream task performance, and reduces authorship attribution risk relative to the original student-written texts, including against a dedicated authorship-attribution model.

title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
summary: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.

title: Diversity in Unity, Theory in Practice: Hierarchical Multitask Benchmarks for Chinese Minority Languages
summary: Despite the rapid advancement of LLMs, their performance on linguistically and culturally diverse minority languages within a unified national context remains underexplored. We present CMiLBench, a collection of hierarchical multitask benchmarks designed to translate theoretical notions of "diversity in unity" into practical evaluation for three representative Chinese minority languages: Tibetan, Mongolian, and Uyghur. CMiLBench comprises 24,663 instances across 5 difficulty levels and 17 tasks spanning foundational ability, cultural specificity, and safety alignment. We adopt existing dataset adaptation, minority knowledge construction, and high-resource benchmark translation to construct CMiLBench. We assess 14 state-of-the-art commercial and open-source LLMs with a hybrid framework that integrates automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring. The comparative experimental results reveal the gap between theoretical capability and practical utility. CMiLBench serves as a foundational and scalable evaluation resource to bridge the digital language divide and promote the informatization and intelligentization of low-resource Chinese minority languages.

title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
summary: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work, we propose Psychology-based Chain-of-Thought (PsyCoT) reasoning, a theory-driven prompting strategy grounded in the Schachter-Singer and Cognitive Appraisal theories of emotion. We propose and evaluate PsyCoT for subjective NLP tasks, including emotion analysis, emotion intensity prediction, stress analysis, and depression severity identification. Our evaluation covers four levels of classification complexity: binary, multiclass, multi-label, and ordinal scaling, spanning 11 languages. We assess the performance of five state-of-the-art LLMs across these selected subjective NLP tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PsyCoT prompt variants improve the standard chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting across the evaluated tasks. Across all evaluated tasks, PsyCoT yields F1 score gains ranging from 0.5% to 28.1%, depending on the model, task, and language configuration.

title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
summary: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents
summary: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.

title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity
summary: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.

title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
summary: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
summary: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

title: Think Before You Forecast: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.

title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.

title: CompareDR: Benchmarking Deep Research Reports from Individual Quality to Comparative Merit
summary: Deep research systems can produce reports with different evidence, analyses, and conclusions for the same query. A reader deciding which findings to rely on needs to know how well each report meets the task requirements and which differences matter to the answer. A score for a single report can summarize its quality, but it does not identify which contributions make one report more useful than another. We introduce CompareDR, a benchmark that combines task-specific pointwise audits with guideline-based pairwise comparisons. We use passage-linked report representations to locate relevant differences and selective evidence verification to check claims that could affect the judgment. The benchmark comprises 40 Chinese and English tasks from three existing benchmarks, 360 reports from nine systems, 1,099 human-reviewed evaluation criteria, and human preferences elicited through blinded comparisons of 80 report pairs. The hybrid evaluator matches 69 of these 80 preferences (86.25%, Cohen's $κ=0.746$). The benchmark supports both comparisons of research systems and examination of the evidence and analyses behind those judgments.

title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
summary: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
summary: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
summary: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.

title: Meddies-PII: A Multilingual Framework for Personally Identifiable Information Extraction in Clinical De-identification
summary: Multilingual PII extraction in clinical text is limited by scarce governed data and by synthetic corpora whose construction is thinly documented. We present a large multilingual dataset covering seventeen languages, including seven Southeast Asian languages, and nine PII labels. We also document a detailed generation pipeline and release the complete prompts, catalogues, checks and label maps. A compact 350M-parameter BIOES token classifier trained on the resource achieves the highest score on all fifteen public benchmarks, significantly ahead of the strongest of four public systems on fourteen of them, with a mean exact-match F1 of 0.827 against 0.672 for the strongest system. We also tested it, without adaptation, on multilingual benchmarks, including two human-annotated German and Spanish clinical-style corpora, where it is competitive with the best public systems once annotation conventions are aligned, and is best in four of ten MultiGraSCCo languages; the results show that performance transfers across public benchmarks. We also analyse the data and find almost no near-duplicates and no text overlap between training and any evaluation set. The dataset, benchmark, model, generation framework and evaluation code are planned for public release upon acceptance.

title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
summary: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.

title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images
summary: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
summary: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding
summary: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.

title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
summary: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
summary: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
summary: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
summary: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.

title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates
summary: When a large language model (LLM) is updated, its developer must decide whether accuracy improved, worsened or stayed within a tolerance. An LLM judge can assess every prompt cheaply but imperfectly, while human labels are costly. We propose Sequential Decisions with Optimal Labelling Designs (SOLD), which labels one prompt at a time, uses the judge to correct the estimate of the change in accuracy and to choose the prompts, and stops once the evidence is conclusive. A wrong decision has probability at most a prespecified level whenever labelling stops. The commonly used Neyman allocation minimises the variance of the estimate and therefore rarely labels prompts that the judge is confident about. It can need far more draws when the outcomes of these prompts could still fall far below the judge's prediction. We instead derive the design that gathers evidence fastest, which labels each prompt with probability at least proportional to how far its outcome could fall below the prediction. As the level tends to zero, no procedure based on the judge-corrected estimates needs fewer draws than SOLD. In simulations and on the EVOUNA and MMLU-Pro datasets, SOLD needed fewer labels than the other methods.

title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling
summary: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. We introduce context-aware \textbf{BQVAE} for scalar quantization of DNA and \textbf{BQDNA}, an autoregressive gLM supporting multi-head codebooks. Comprehensive experiments reveal that: (1) unique training dynamics of vector quantization in DNA space, including the importance of alignment between training corpus and downstream data. (2) superior performance of BQVAE over hand-crafted tokenizers and vanilla VQVAE. (3) remarkable cross-species generalization capability of BQDNA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance with merely 0.1B multi-species training for BQVAE and 1 epoch training on hg38 for BQDNA, outperforming gLMs pretrained with 10$\sim$100x more tokens. Our findings underscore the potential of learned vector quantization for genomic sequence representation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/BQDNA

title: Can Speech LLMs Recognize When Audio Evidence Is Insufficient? A Diagnostic Study and a Pre-Generation Probing Mitigation
summary: Speech large language models are usually evaluated on questions that have answers. We ask what they do when a recording establishes none, and whether the standard way of finding out is sound. Diagnosed on synthesized speech the answer looks clear: Qwen2-Audio fabricates an answer to 92.5% of unanswerable questions, while an ASR cascade reading the same recordings reaches 2.5% hallucination at 6.7% over-refusal, placing the failure in reasoning rather than in perception. The identical protocol on 376 native SQuAD 2.0 questions over human-read recordings removes that conclusion: the cascade hallucinates on 67.7% against the end-to-end model's 69.8%, at a higher over-refusal cost. A paired subset asking the same questions of a synthesized and a human recording of each passage localises the effect in the ASR stage -- the end-to-end model's abstention behaviour does not move with the speaker, the cascade's goes from 11.1% to 65.9%.
